content: Ultrasonography has been investigated as a method to confirm the correct placement of gastric tubes, which are commonly used for administering medications and providing nutrition to individuals who cannot swallow. Misplacement of these tubes into the trachea can lead to severe complications, such as pneumonia. Therefore, ensuring proper placement of the tube in the stomach is critical. Recent research has suggested that ultrasonography may offer high diagnostic accuracy for this purpose and could serve as a viable alternative to X-rays, particularly in settings where X-ray facilities are unavailable or difficult to access. The objective of this systematic review was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasonography, either alone or in combination with other methods, for confirming gastric tube placement in both children and adults. This review is an update of a previously published Cochrane review. For the update, databases such as the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, Embase, and others were searched up to April 2023, and study authors were contacted for additional data. The review included studies that assessed the diagnostic accuracy of nasogastric and orogastric tube placement using ultrasonography, with X-ray visualization as the reference standard. Only cross-sectional and case-control studies were included, while case series, case reports, and studies without X-ray as the reference standard were excluded. Studies involving gastrostomy or enteric tubes were also excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality of the included studies and extracted data. Authors of the studies were contacted to obtain missing information. Due to limited data on specificity, the meta-analysis focused on sensitivity, using a univariate random-effects logistic regression model to combine data from studies employing similar methods and echo windows. The review identified 12 new studies in addition to 10 studies from the earlier version, resulting in a total of 22 studies involving 1939 participants and 1944 tube insertions. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was judged to be low or unclear, but no study was found to have a low risk of bias across all domains of the QUADAS-2 tool. Data on specificity were sparse, with only 152 participants available for analysis, due to the low incidence of tube misplacement. The pooled sensitivity of ultrasonography using neck and abdominal echo windows was 96% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 92% to 98%) for air injection and 98% (95% CI: 83% to 100%) for saline injection, both with moderate-certainty evidence. For abdominal echo windows alone, the sensitivity was 96% (95% CI: 65% to 100%) for air injection (very low-certainty evidence) and 97% (95% CI: 95% to 99%) for procedures without injection (moderate-certainty evidence). However, the certainty of evidence for specificity across all methods was very low due to the small sample size. In settings where X-ray was not readily available, eight studies involving 552 participants reported that the sensitivity of ultrasonography combined with other confirmatory tests ranged from 86% to 98%, with specificity estimates of 100% but wide confidence intervals. For nine studies involving 782 participants that assessed ultrasonography alone, sensitivity ranged from 77% to 98%, while specificity was either 100% with wide confidence intervals or not estimable due to the absence of misplacement events. The authors concluded that, based on the limited evidence available, ultrasonography does not have sufficient accuracy to serve as a standalone test for confirming gastric tube placement. However, in situations where X-ray is not accessible, ultrasonography may be a useful tool for detecting misplaced gastric tubes. Larger studies are needed to better evaluate the potential for adverse events associated with the use of ultrasonography for this purpose.
